pedagogy.summary: Ordering and continuing patterns and sequences develops from duplicating and extending by visual matching to abstracting the UNIT OF REPEAT and identifying the smallest repeating unit — and only these last two mark genuine understanding rather than surface matching (Rittle-Johnson et al. 2013). Teaching should move children beyond 'what comes next' to seeing a pattern as made of repeating units: naming and circling the unit, recreating a pattern with different materials (abstraction, which cannot be done by visual matching), and asking for the smallest arrangement that keeps the pattern.
bestPractices: Shift the focus from 'what comes next' to structure: name and circle the unit of repeat, not just append the next item.
Use abstraction tasks — recreate the same kind of pattern with different materials or colours — which force attention to structure because visual matching won't work.
Ask for the smallest unit ('what is the smallest tower that still keeps the pattern?') to assess unit identification, the hardest and most telling skill.
Include units beyond simple AB (ABB, AAB, ABC), because children over-rely on alternation; watch for them reverting to AB.
Model 'same, same, different' language and 'start over' framing to make the repeating unit explicit.
keyRepresentations: The unit of repeat circled or boxed
ABB / AAB units contrasted with AB
'Same, same, different' labelling of the unit
Number sequences and skip-counting as patterns
commonMisconceptions: Extends a pattern by visually matching and appending the last item, without grasping that there is a repeating unit.
Reverts to a simple AB pattern when the model unit is longer (makes ABAB for an ABB model).
Produces a partially correct pattern — one full unit plus extra items that break the unit.

learn.summary: Patterns and sequences teaching should move children beyond 'what comes next' to seeing a pattern as made of a repeating UNIT. The telling skills are abstracting a pattern onto new materials and identifying the smallest repeating unit — both of which, according to Rittle-Johnson et al. (2013), cannot be done by visual matching alone and so reveal genuine structural understanding rather than surface copying. Build, extend, abstract, and isolate the unit, using units beyond simple AB (ABB, AAB, ABC) because children over-rely on alternation.

activities.title: Build, extend, and name the unit of repeat
feedback: If the child only appends the last item without a sense of the unit, label the model with 'same' and 'different' and box the repeating chunk, then rebuild from that unit before extending.
If they produce one full unit then stray cubes that break it, treat this as emerging knowledge, not simply wrong: ask 'where does the pattern start again?' and practise shorter units first.
Prompt: 'Point to the part of the pattern that repeats — where does it start again?'
activities.rationale: Economopoulos (quoted in Rittle-Johnson et al.) argues children must move from seeing a pattern as a sequence of 'what comes next' to analysing its structure as repeating units in order to generalise and predict. Naming and circling the unit makes that structure explicit.
sourceClaims: To generalise and predict, children must move from looking at a pattern as a sequence of 'what comes next' to analysing its structure — seeing that it is made of repeating units (Economopoulos, 1998, quoted in the study).
learnerActions: Continue a given model pattern, e.g. red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue — carry it on further with cubes, beads, or drawn shapes.
Circle or box the part that repeats and say where the pattern 'starts over'.

Name which items are the SAME and which is DIFFERENT: for red, blue, blue the two blues are the same and the red is the different cube that starts the chunk (spoken in order: different, same, same). The plain 'same, same, different' chant maps most cleanly to a two-same-then-different unit such as AAB.
activities.intendedInsight: A repeating pattern is built from a unit that repeats; the pattern is the unit, not just the next item you could add.

activities.title: Abstract the same KIND of pattern onto new materials
feedback: If the child reverts to green-yellow-green-yellow (AB) for an ABB model, lay the new pattern under the model and check unit-for-unit; count how many yellows come before the next green.
If they merely copy surface colours or cannot reproduce the structure on new materials, return to boxing the unit in the model and rebuild from that chunk.
Prompt: 'Is your green-and-yellow pattern the SAME KIND as the red-and-blue one? How can you check?'
activities.rationale: Rittle-Johnson et al. report that abstracting a pattern onto new materials is a harder skill than extending, cannot be done by visual matching, and clearly demonstrates understanding; children commonly revert to AB for longer units, so non-AB models (ABB, AAB) are important.
sourceClaims: Children can often duplicate and extend repeating patterns by visual matching without knowing there is a pattern unit that repeats; abstracting a pattern onto new materials and identifying the smallest unit of repeat are harder skills that cannot be done by visual matching and are the ones that clearly demonstrate understanding. Common errors include reverting to a simple AB pattern for a longer unit and producing one full unit plus extraneous items; longer units are harder to preserve.
learnerActions: Given a red-blue-blue model, use a different set (e.g. green and yellow cubes) to make 'the same KIND of pattern' — green, yellow, yellow, repeated.
Lay the new pattern directly under the model and check unit-for-unit: count how many yellows come before the next green.
Explain why your new pattern is the same kind even though the colours are different.
activities.intendedInsight: Making the 'same kind' of pattern means reproducing the STRUCTURE (one cube, then two matching cubes, then start over), not the colours — abstraction that colour matching alone cannot accomplish.

activities.title: Shrink to the smallest tower that keeps the pattern
feedback: If the child offers a longer stretch than one unit, ask them to take away cubes one whole unit at a time until only one copy of the unit is left (taking away more would break it). Then check that it still has the full arrangement: for red-blue-blue, the red that starts it and then the two matching blues; for AAB, two matching cubes then a different one; for ABC, three different cubes.
Prompt: 'If I take some cubes away, is it still the same pattern? Why?' and 'What is the smallest tower you could build that still has this pattern?'
Watch for reverting to AB on longer units; if it happens, return to the unit-for-unit check from the abstraction task.
activities.rationale: Rittle-Johnson et al. identify smallest-unit identification as the hardest and most telling patterning skill, not achievable by visual matching. Including units beyond AB counters children's over-reliance on alternation.
sourceClaims: Children can often duplicate and extend repeating patterns by visual matching without knowing there is a pattern unit that repeats; abstracting a pattern onto new materials and identifying the smallest unit of repeat are harder skills that cannot be done by visual matching and are the ones that clearly demonstrate understanding. Common errors include reverting to a simple AB pattern for a longer unit and producing one full unit plus extraneous items; longer units are harder to preserve.
learnerActions: From a repeating pattern, build the smallest tower that still has the same pattern (for red-blue-blue, the three-cube unit red, blue, blue).
Decide whether removing cubes keeps or breaks the pattern, and explain why.
Try the same with AAB and ABC units, not just AB.
activities.intendedInsight: The smallest arrangement that preserves the pattern IS the unit of repeat; isolating it is the clearest sign of understanding structure.

activities.title: Describe the rule and connect to number sequences
feedback: If the rule given is only 'the next one is blue', press for the whole unit and where it restarts.
If a self-made 'longer' pattern collapses to AB, prompt the unit-for-unit check before they hand it over.
Encourage children to say which items are the same and which are different (for an ABC unit, all three are different), and to use 'start over' language, to make the unit clear.
activities.rationale: The micro-topic requires describing rules and creating patterns. Using 'same/different' and 'start over' language makes the repeating unit clear. Number sequences and skip-counting can be linked as rule-based patterns, but their rule is a repeated step (e.g. add 2), not a repeating unit of items, and this difference should be pointed out.
sourceClaims: To generalise and predict, children must move from looking at a pattern as a sequence of 'what comes next' to analysing its structure — seeing that it is made of repeating units (Economopoulos, 1998, quoted in the study).
learnerActions: Say aloud the rule for a given sequence of objects ('it goes red, then two blues, then starts over').

Look at number sequences and skip-counting as patterns too, but notice the difference: in skip-counting (2, 4, 6, 8, …) the numbers keep growing and do not repeat, but the step does (add 2 each time). Some parts can repeat like a unit, e.g. the last digits when counting in 5s (5, 10, 15, 20 → 5, 0, 5, 0).
Create your own pattern with a chosen unit (ABB, AAB, or ABC) and challenge someone else to find the smallest unit.
activities.intendedInsight: Saying the rule out loud and making your own patterns help children move from 'what comes next' to thinking about the repeating unit. Number sequences such as skip-counting are a different kind of pattern: the numbers grow, and what repeats is the rule or step (e.g. +2), not a unit of items.

constraints: A static pattern with the unit highlighted (e.g. tap to box the unit and reveal which items are same/different) is a useful reference, but a fixed display on its own does not let the child extend, abstract, or isolate the unit; pair it with building/doing tasks.

Sequence and fill-in-the-blank response formats can check 'what comes next' and 'circle the unit', but risk rewarding visual matching; always add an abstraction (new-materials) task and a smallest-unit task to go beyond appending.
Extending a pattern can be achieved by visual matching without understanding; use the abstraction and smallest-unit tasks to distinguish surface copying from structural understanding.
Use units beyond AB (ABB, AAB, ABC) because children over-rely on alternation and may revert to AB on longer units.
A partially correct pattern (one full unit plus stray items) is a transitional, emerging state — do not treat it as simply wrong.

The 'same, same, different' chant describes a two-same-then-different unit (AAB); for the ABB example (red, blue, blue) name the two blues as the same and the red as the different start rather than chanting the phrase in order over it.

Optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete: swapping to a new colour set for the abstraction task, a 'shrink to the smallest tower' control, laying the new pattern under the model for unit-for-unit comparison, and flagging reversions to AB. These are suggestions, not required mechanisms.

Hands-on construction is central for building and abstracting patterns; conversation can support prompting an explanation of the rule alongside that construction, without being treated as a substitute for it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated 3D as adding nothing and conversation/static image as poor. These have been softened: patterning structure is not inherently spatial, and a fixed display or dialogue can still support reference and explanation respectively. No comparative efficacy or necessity claim is asserted beyond the specific source claim that extending can be done by visual matching while abstraction and smallest-unit identification cannot.
The claim that abstraction and smallest-unit tasks 'cannot be done by visual matching' is attributed to Rittle-Johnson et al. (2013) and retained as sourced, not generalised beyond it.

The original row applied 'same, same, different' to its red-blue-blue (ABB) example, which read in order is different-same-same. The learner-facing text now names which items are same and which is different instead of chanting the phrase over ABB, so the label and example no longer disagree; the phrase is noted as fitting an AAB unit.
Example pattern (red, blue, blue = ABB; green, yellow, yellow abstraction; three-cube smallest unit) checked for internal consistency and found coherent.

probeDeeper: Point to the part of the pattern that repeats — where does it start again?
Is your green-and-yellow pattern the SAME KIND as the red-and-blue one? How can you check?
What is the smallest tower you could build that still has this pattern?
If I take some cubes away, is it still the same pattern? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: Extends the pattern preserving the red-blue-blue unit; abstracts the ABB structure into green-yellow-yellow (neither reverting to an AB alternation nor merely copying the colours); and offers the three-cube unit (green, yellow, yellow) as the smallest tower that keeps the pattern.

responseLevels.gap: Appends items by matching the last one; on new materials reverts to AB or copies colours — no sense of a unit.
responseLevels.full: Extends, abstracts to new materials, and identifies the smallest unit of repeat for multi-element units, explaining the pattern as a repeating unit rather than 'what comes next'.
responseLevels.partial: Extends and often abstracts familiar AB patterns, but breaks down on longer units (ABB/AAB) — reverting to AB or adding extra items — and cannot isolate the smallest unit.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a pattern made with coloured cubes: red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue. First, carry it on for me. Now, using these different cubes (green and yellow), make the same KIND of pattern. Last, show me the smallest tower you could make that still keeps the same pattern.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Extending alone can be done by visual matching; the abstraction task (new materials) and the 'smallest unit' task cannot. A child who only appends by look reverts to AB or copies surface colours; a child who holds the unit reproduces the ABB structure and isolates the three-cube unit. The three tasks together separate visual matching from structural understanding.
